title: Self-service password reset (SSPR)
learningObjective: Set up self-service password reset (SSPR): who can use it, which methods they need, how they register, and writeback to on-premises. Explain why a user can or can't reset their password.
foundation: SSPR lets users reset a forgotten password themselves, without calling the help desk.

You choose who can use it (no one, a selected group, or everyone), how many verification methods they must pass (one or two), and which methods are allowed (authenticator app, text or call, email, security questions…).
Users must register their methods first, and you can require them to register the next time they sign in.
Administrators are always covered by a stricter built-in policy, whatever you choose for users.
engineer: Who can use SSPR: None; Selected, meaning one group (good for a pilot); All.
Licences: SSPR for cloud users needs Entra ID P1 or a Microsoft 365 business plan that includes it. Password writeback for synced users also needs P1.
Methods users can pick from: Microsoft Authenticator (notification or code); mobile phone (SMS or voice call); office phone; email; security questions. You choose whether users need 1 or 2 methods.
Security questions: they are the weakest method. Admins can never use them.
Admins always get a stricter policy: it is on for every Azure admin role, whatever you set for users. Admins need two methods, and security questions aren't allowed.

Registration: turn on 'Require users to register when signing in'. Users are asked to confirm their details again every 180 days by default (you can change this). Combined registration lets users set up SSPR and MFA methods in one go.
Notifications: tell users when their password is reset. Tell all admins when another admin resets theirs. You can also add a help-desk link or email to the reset page.

Synced (hybrid) users: SSPR needs password writeback for them. Without it, the cloud can't change their on-premises password, so the reset fails. With writeback, the on-premises password rules (complexity, history) apply too. Turn it on in Entra Connect or Cloud Sync.

One place for methods: since 30 September 2025, the methods allowed for both MFA and SSPR are set in the Authentication methods policy (Protection > Authentication methods > Policies). The old MFA and SSPR method settings no longer decide which methods users can use.

animation.caption: Open the SSPR tab: change scope, methods and writeback, then test each user.

example.title: Try it with a group first, then everyone
body: Contoso turns on SSPR for the group 'SSPR pilot'. Users need two methods: the Authenticator app and a mobile phone. Users must register when they sign in. Password writeback is on, because most users are synced from AD.
After two quiet weeks, Contoso changes the scope to All. Security questions stay off, because the security team says they are too weak.

prerequisites: Entra ID P1, or a Microsoft 365 plan that includes it
For synced users: Entra Connect or Cloud Sync with password writeback
permissions: Authentication Policy Administrator or Global Administrator, to set up password reset
Hybrid Identity Administrator, to set up writeback in Entra Connect or Cloud Sync
portal: Microsoft Entra admin center > Protection > Password reset > Properties: Self service password reset enabled = None / Selected / All (choose the group for Selected).
Authentication methods: number of methods required and the allowed methods.
Registration: require users to register when signing in; days before users are asked to reconfirm.
On-premises integration: enable password writeback (requires Connect or Cloud Sync).
Notifications and Customization: user/admin notifications and help-desk link.
configuration.cli:
# SSPR policy is configured in the Microsoft Entra admin center; there is no az command for it.
# Inspect a user's registered authentication methods through Microsoft Graph:
az rest --method get --url https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/users/ana@contoso.com/authentication/methods
configuration.powershell:
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'UserAuthenticationMethod.Read.All'
Get-MgUserAuthenticationMethod -UserId 'ana@contoso.com' | Select-Object Id, AdditionalProperties
# Registration status across users (requires Reports.Read.All)
Get-MgReportAuthenticationMethodUserRegistrationDetail | Select-Object UserPrincipalName, IsSsprRegistered, IsSsprCapable

lab.objective: Explain every SSPR success and failure from scope, methods, writeback and the admin policy.
steps: On the SSPR tab, try Ana (in the pilot group, but only one method registered). Register a second method and try again.
Try Chen (synced) with writeback off, then turn writeback on and add Chen to scope by switching to All.
Try Dana (Global Admin) with security questions registered. Then register Authenticator app and mobile phone.
expected: Admins need two methods and cannot use security questions

validation.text: Saw a reset blocked and read why

failureScenarios: Scope set to Selected with the user outside the group
lab.cost: None in the simulation. SSPR needs P1 (or an eligible Microsoft 365 plan) in a real tenant.

troubleshooting.symptom: The user sees 'Your account is not enabled for password reset'.
troubleshooting.cause: SSPR is set to None, or to Selected and the user isn't in that group.
troubleshooting.fix: Add the user to the group, or change the scope.

troubleshooting.symptom: The reset works in the cloud, but the old password still works on-premises.
troubleshooting.cause: Password writeback is off or failing.
troubleshooting.fix: Turn on writeback in Entra Connect or Cloud Sync, and in Password reset > On-premises integration.

troubleshooting.symptom: An admin can't use security questions.
troubleshooting.cause: The admin policy never allows them.
troubleshooting.fix: Register two strong methods (app, phone or email).

troubleshooting.symptom: A user is asked to register again.
troubleshooting.fix: This is normal. Change 'Number of days before users are asked to re-confirm' if you want.

comparisons.difference: Changing a password you know works for every cloud user. Resetting a password you forgot is SSPR.
Users can reset their own password for its directory. Entra SSPR adds method rules and writeback to on-premises AD.

misconceptions.myth: Turning SSPR off for users also turns it off for admins.
misconceptions.reality: No. Admins always have SSPR, with the two-method policy.

misconceptions.myth: SSPR works for synced users straight away.
misconceptions.reality: No. Synced users need password writeback.

misconceptions.myth: 'Selected' scope means you pick individual users.
misconceptions.reality: No. You pick one group, and its members can use SSPR.

architectureDecisions: Start with a pilot group: test SSPR on one group, then turn it on for All.
Ask for two strong methods: prefer the Authenticator app over text messages, and leave security questions off.
Use combined registration: users set up MFA and SSPR methods once, in one place.

walkthrough.subtitle: Let people reset their own forgotten password, safely, without calling the help desk.

steps.label: Locked out
steps.title: Monday 8 a.m.: Ana forgot her password
body: She calls the help desk, waits 20 minutes, and someone resets it by hand. Multiply that by a large company and it costs real money.

steps.label: SSPR
steps.title: Self-service password reset
body: With SSPR, Ana goes to aka.ms/sspr, proves who she is with a second method, and chooses a new password herself.
Resetting a forgotten password needs Microsoft Entra ID P1 (or a Microsoft 365 business licence). Changing a password you still know is free.

steps.label: Scope
steps.title: Turn it on for nobody, some, or everyone
body: Password reset > Properties: None, Selected (one security group) or All. Start with a pilot group, then move to All.
Administrators are always enabled with a stronger two-method policy, whatever you choose here.

steps.label: Methods
steps.title: How users prove who they are
body: Choose 1 or 2 methods required to reset. Methods include the Microsoft Authenticator app, email, mobile phone and security questions. Microsoft now manages which methods are allowed in the Authentication methods policy.
Registration: require users to register their methods at sign-in, and re-confirm them every N days. Notifications tell users and admins when a password is reset.

callout.text: Two methods required is more secure than one. Security questions are the weakest method.

steps.label: Test
steps.title: Case: Ana resets her own password
body: Ana signs in once, registers the Authenticator app and her phone. A week later she forgets her password, opens aka.ms/sspr, confirms both methods and sets a new one in two minutes.

steps.label: Recap
steps.title: SSPR in one minute
body: Users fix their own passwords; you choose who and how.
recap: Reset of forgotten passwords needs Entra ID P1
Scope: None, Selected (one group) or All
Users register methods, then reset at aka.ms/sspr
Admins always have SSPR with two methods

handsOn.title: Turn on SSPR for a group and reset a password as Ana
handsOn.cost: Free with the Entra ID P2 trial from the licences lab.
before: Signed in at portal.azure.com with the account that created your Azure subscription. That account is a Global Administrator of its own Microsoft Entra tenant.
The P2 trial is active and grp-it-lab (with Ana Lab) has the licence.
Ana's sign-in name and the temporary password you copied.

steps.do: Open Microsoft Entra ID > Password reset > Properties. Set 'Self service password reset enabled' to Selected, choose grp-it-lab, and select Save.
Select Authentication methods. Set 'Number of methods required to reset' to 1 and tick Email and Mobile phone. Save.
steps.tip: In some tenants the methods list is managed in Protection > Authentication methods > Policies. If the page sends you there, enable Email OTP there.

steps.do: Select Registration. Set 'Require users to register when signing in' to Yes. Save.
Open a private (InPrivate/Incognito) browser window and sign in at myapps.microsoft.com as Ana with the temporary password. Set a new password when asked.
steps.see: A prompt asking Ana to register security information.
steps.tip: Use My Apps rather than the Azure portal: Azure now requires multifactor authentication for portal sign-in, which adds extra set-up steps.

steps.do: Register an email address you can read (or a phone number). Finish and close the browser.
steps.see: A confirmation that the method is registered.

steps.do: Open another private window, go to aka.ms/sspr and enter Ana's sign-in name. Complete the check with the code sent to the email or phone.
steps.see: A page to choose a new password.

steps.do: Set a new password and sign in with it.
steps.see: Ana signs in successfully. Admins can see the event in Password reset > Audit logs.

check: Ana reset her own password without an admin.
Password reset > Audit logs shows the reset.
cleanup: Set Password reset > Properties back to None when you finish if you like. Nothing here costs money.
